The idea

Teaching a machine to “mind surf.”

Surfers on the beach watch the water and imagine their line before paddling out. This project teaches a model to do the same — one frame at a time.

Every surfer knows the ocean’s mood swings: one day you’re catching the perfect line, the next you’re flattened by a six-foot breaker and tumbled like laundry. I spent six weeks chasing waves in Bali and Sri Lanka — wipeouts and all — because nothing beats carving your own pocket.

It all comes down to the fundamentals: positioning yourself in the pocket of the wave, where speed and control meet. That spark led me here — to build a computer-vision model that tracks the pocket frame by frame, helping surfers visualize their best line before they even paddle out.

pocket · the target zone

The pocket is the steep, powerful zone just ahead of where the wave breaks — the region this model is trained to detect.

01 · Data collection

From surf clips to labeled frames.

I gathered footage from Surfline, focused on the Canggu, Bali beach break — my favourite spot, and one whose mix of left- and right-breaking waves is perfect for teaching a model to recognize pockets in both directions.

Canggu, Bali — left- and right-breaking waves highlighted in red.

Using FFmpeg, I converted each MP4 clip into a sequence of 1280×720 frames at 1 fps, then batch-uploaded them to Roboflow for annotation. The extraction loop from upload_to_roboflow.ipynb:

import os, glob, subprocess

HOME = os.getcwd()
base_dir = f"{HOME}/content/video_to_upload"
output_base = f"{HOME}/content/extracted_frames"
mp4_files = glob.glob(f"{base_dir}/*.mp4")

for filepath in sorted(mp4_files):
    filename = os.path.splitext(os.path.basename(filepath))[0]
    out_dir = os.path.join(output_base, filename)
    os.makedirs(out_dir, exist_ok=True)
    pattern = os.path.join(out_dir, "frame_%04d.png")
    subprocess.run([
        "ffmpeg", "-hide_banner", "-loglevel", "error",
        "-i", filepath, "-vf", "fps=1", "-q:v", "1",
        "-pix_fmt", "rgb24", pattern
    ], check=True)

02 · Data labeling

2,077 frames, ~3,000 pockets, by hand.

I annotated every pocket in Roboflow, then split the set 70 / 20 / 10 into train / validation / test — randomly, so each split fairly represents the different pocket types.

What’s a train / validation / test split?

Training set (70%) — the model sees these and adjusts its parameters to learn the task.

Validation set (20%) — checked during training to gauge performance on unseen data and tune things like learning rate.

Test set (10%) — held back until the very end; the true measure of performance on brand-new data.

Before export I ran Auto-Orient to strip hidden EXIF orientation tags, then downsampled every image to 640×640 — smaller, faster, still detailed enough for pocket detection. Finally I exported to YOLOv8 TXT format: an images/ folder of .jpg files beside a labels/ folder of matching .txt files.

Contents of the YOLOv8 PyTorch TXT export.

Each label line is class_id x_center y_center width height. Because “pocket” is the only class, class_id is always 0, and all five numbers are normalized to 0–1 so annotations stay consistent at any resolution. A data.yaml ties the splits together with nc: 1 and the class name pocket.

03 · Model development

Fine-tuning YOLOv8-nano.

I started from YOLOv8-nano — the smallest of the five variants (225 layers, ~3M parameters), pre-trained on COCO’s 80 classes. I added a single pocket class and adjusted the weights to detect it. The full script lives in train_model_with_custom_dataset.ipynb.

Training ran as a detection task for up to 40 epochs, with early stopping (patience 10), inputs resized to 512×512, batch size 16. I validated on the 20% split, then evaluated on the held-out 10% test set at a 0.3 confidence threshold. The resulting best.pt weights were deployed via the Roboflow API for inference on new footage.

04 · Performance analysis

Predictions that hug the ground truth.

First, a visual gut-check on the validation set — manual labels on the left, the model’s predictions on the right. The bounding boxes line up closely, at high confidence.

Explore the metrics

Five views of how the detector behaves across confidence thresholds.

What it shows

Confusion matrix

A 2×2 table of true / false positives and negatives on the validation set.

Why it matters — 516 pockets correctly detected against 64 misses and only 13 false alarms tells us exactly where the model errs, and whether to gather more edge cases or adjust thresholds.

What it shows

F1 · confidence curve

F1 score — the harmonic mean of precision and recall — across confidence thresholds.

Why it matters — the peak of 0.93 around threshold 0.38 is the sweet spot where detections are both accurate and comprehensive — key for live surf-cam inference.

What it shows

Precision · confidence curve

Precision — correct detections over total detections — across confidence thresholds.

Why it matters — precision reaching 1.00 by 0.86 confidence means high-confidence predictions are nearly all real pockets, guiding a safe cutoff to minimize false alerts.

What it shows

Precision · recall curve (mAP@0.5)

The trade-off between precision and recall, summarized by area under the curve.

Why it matters — an mAP of 0.959 signals outstanding detection quality — the model reliably finds pockets even as thresholds vary, crucial in changing wave conditions.

What it shows

Recall · confidence curve

Recall — the true-positive rate — across confidence thresholds.

Why it matters — recall staying above 0.89 below 0.80 confidence means most pockets are caught early, so the threshold can be tuned to miss very few.

05 · Real-time inference

The model, let loose on new footage.

Four clips it had never seen — from the home break to a world tour event to my own session. Each plays on loop; every coral box is a live pocket detection.

inference
Canggu, Bali · trained break

Home break, unseen clip.

Applied to a never-before-seen Canggu video — the same break as the training data. The model consistently nails both left- and right-hand pockets, frame after frame. Reliable first-pass detections like these show it generalizes to fresh footage.

inference
Pipeline, Hawaii · unseen break

A break it was never trained on.

Tested on world-famous Pipeline — a location absent from training. It still identifies most left-hand pockets and many subtler right-hand ones. A few gentle right pockets slip through, but overall it holds up, showing strong cross-break generalization.

inference
Bells Beach · WSL Rip Curl Pro 2025

Stress-tested on competition surf.

Pushed further onto WSL footage of Kanoa Igarashi (also my favourite surfer 😂) at Bells Beach. Despite heavy whitewash and much larger waves, it pinpoints the pocket zones — a pleasant surprise I hadn’t expected.

inference
Bonus · my own session

Low-res, heavy whitewash — still locked on.

A final run on a clip of my own surf session. Despite the low resolution and churn, it holds onto the main pocket zones — though it amusingly mistook me for a pocket once. Room to refine, but solid under tough conditions.

What’s next

Sharper models, bigger ideas.

Potential improvements

  • Switch to a larger YOLOv8 variant (small or medium) for richer feature extraction.
  • Train on full-resolution frames instead of 512×512 crops to preserve wave detail.
  • Expand the dataset beyond 2,000 images with diverse wave types, lighting, and weather.
  • Increase training epochs — watch mAP for the point of diminishing returns.
  • Systematic hyperparameter tuning (learning rate, augmentations) for optimal performance.

Future applications

  • Interactive surf coaching — overlay pocket zones on a surfer’s own video for real-time feedback.
  • Smart surf cameras — track ride duration, catch/miss ratio, and show the live pocket at any break.
  • Session analytics — aggregate detections across a session, score performance, and chart progress over time.

Thanks for reading

Pocket detection can grow into a whole suite of surf-training and beach-monitoring tools. Ideas and feedback are always welcome.
